To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a notable proportion of hypercholesterolemics and hypertensives without symptomatic cardiovascular diseases may have a required risk reduction that is greater than the achievable risk reduction offered by cholesterol-lowering or anti-hypertensive medication, implying that decision-aid interventions may help individuals clarify their preferences about accepting or refusing medication for the primary-prevention of cardiovascular diseases.

a substantial proportion of patients in primary prevention of cardiovascular diseases may not accept medication even if they are offered the maximal risk reduction possible and a significant proportion of patients in this population may have risk reduction requirements that are considerably higher than the risk reduction achievable through medication.

18-37% of patients without symptomatic coronary heart disease or cerebrovascular disease who are at increased risk for these conditions are unwilling to accept drug therapy to reduce their risk, and that another 28-37% are unwilling to accept the risk reduction that drug therapy could provide.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether the benefits of drug therapy in primary prevention of cardiovascular diseases are sufficiently great to justify the risks of the drugs and the inconvenience of taking them for many years.
the development of a new method for estimating patients’ preferences for risk reduction.
how patients’ preferences can be incorporated into decisions about the initiation of primary prevention drug therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the primary prevention of CVD with drug therapy is a complex process that requires a careful and detailed assessment of the individual patient’s risk, benefits and preferences.

there is no evidence that the use of primary prevention drug therapy in patients with cardiovascular disease risk factors can meet their requirements for reduced risk, and that there may be a notable number of patients who are over-requirers.
a notable proportion of primary prevention patients may have a ReqRR that is considerably greater than their achievable risk reduction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need more effective and safe drugs for the primary prevention.
we have shown that there are patients who would refuse any drug treatment for the primary prevention cardiovascular disease.

the use of individual risk estimates in trade-off tasks can be used as a decision aid to help patients and clinicians clarify preferences about accepting or declining medication for primary prevention.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk reduction achieved by medication may not be sufficient for many primary prevention patients.
a substantial number of patients in primary prevention may not be satisfied with the risk reductions offered by current drug therapies.

there may be a notable portion of patients whose “required” risk reduction is considerably more prominent than what is achievable with medication, and that this may be an issue for clinicians to address in the clinical encounter.
